title.narrative: IFC, International Finance Corporation, Access to Finance phase II,2023-2028
IFC, International Finance Corporation, Access to Finance phase II 2023-2028

description.narrative:
Access to Finance fas 2 bygger på framgångar och lärdomar från projektets första fas, som fokuserade på att öka tillgången till finansiering för underfinansierade grupper. Programmet har ett särskilt fokus på små och medelstora företag samt aktörer i Jordbruksvärdekedjan, speciellt kvinnor och kvinnoägda företag, dvs ”de underrepresenterade grupperna”. Programmet bygger vidare på det grundläggande arbetet som har lagts på att åtgärda hinder på utbudssidan (finanssektorn) och på efterfrågesidan (realsektorn). På utbudssidan genom rådgivning och aktiviteter som policyreform, produktutveckling, kapacitetsutveckling av bankerna och innovation kring digital finansiell teknologi. På efterfrågesidan (realsektorn) genom att stärka kompetenser hos låntagare och utvecklingen av kapitalmarknaden.
Programmet har 5 komponenter:
1)Financial Infrastructure
2)Agri supply chain and access to finance
3)MSME banking advisory support
4)Ethiopia capital markets development
5)Environmental, Social and Governance ESG
Programmet avser att genomföra strukturella förändringar och därmed bidra till en hållbar och inkluderande utveckling för tillgång till finansiering. Tillgång till finansiering förväntas leda till utökade ekonomiska möjligheter, ökad produktivitet, ökade arbetstillfällen och i slutändan ha en positiv inverkan på den privata sektorn och på ekonomin i stort.

The Access to Finance Component Phase 2 builds on the successes and learnings from Access to Finance Component Phase 1 Program to increase access to finance for under financed actors, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and agri-value chain actors, with particular focus on smallholder farmers (SHFs), women and youth. The program aims to leverage the foundational work that has been undertaken to address both supply side (financial sector) and demand side (real sector) constraints. Supply side primarily though advisory service for activities such as product development, financer capacitation and financial technology innovation. Demand side (real sector) constraints through borrower literacy, (SMEs) and and capital market development.
The program has five pillars:
1)Financial Infrastructure
2)Agri supply chain and access to finance
3)MSME banking advisory support
4)Ethiopia capital markets development
5)Environmental, Social and Governance ESG
The program seeks to effect structural change and thereby sustainable and inclusive impact on access to finance leading to the expansion of economic opportunities, increased processing capabilities, increased jobs, private sector growth and ultimately impact on the economy at large.

The MDI Access to Finance Phase second phase of the program aims to increase access to finance and thereby economic opportunities for the private sector at large with special focus on small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs); agri-value chain actors ranging from producers, producer organizations to agro-processors (with special focus on women and youth) and women owned businesses i.e. the underserved. The program seeks to effect structural change and thereby sustainable impact on access to finance leading to the expansion of economic opportunities, increased processing capabilities, increases jobs and ultimately impact on the economy at large.
In particular, the program aims to:
*Strengthen and increase financial institutions utilization of the credit information system to enhance the creditworthiness of borrowers and promote the use of their credit histories as collateral complements and substitutes, thus reducing loan collateralization levels.
*Strengthen and increase financial institutions utilization of the MPSR and WRS as tools that would allow them to expand the range of bankable collateral to include movable assets like equipment, purchase orders, accounts receivable, livestock, and commodities, as they are more widely available to marginalized actors and women.
*Leverage digital financial solutions to overcome gaps in bank branch footprints and inefficiencies in loan administration processes.
*Provide hands-on support to financial institutions, including the provision of market analyses, risk appraisals, product design, process enhancement, and go-to-market strategies to boost their understanding and improve their perceptions of opportunities and risks in lending to the underserved via new inclusive financial products and technologies.
*Create and deliver structured financial literacy programs to marginalized actors, including SMEs and agri-value chain actors, with a particular focus on women, in target industries and value chains.
In addition, IFC will lay the foundation for good environmental, social and governance (ESG) practices in the financial and agribusiness sectors to enable a more diversified and resilient economy, and stronger and more sustainable local businesses, which boosts investments.

sector.narrative: Education/training in banking and financial services

description.narrative:
The 2025 reporting demonstrates a clear progression toward more active implementation compared to earlier periods and more catalytical impact of ongoing Pilots. The narrative report highlights advances in advisory engagements, private sector focused reforms, and collaboration with financial institutions and public counterparts. While 2024 reporting emphasised capacity building and institutional readiness, the 2025 report shows emphasis on transactional, financial, and institutional results moving towards scaling of lending products, improved financial infrastructure and more product innovation.
Across the six sectors, the Access to Finance pillar shows strong operational results (especially in agricultural and digital finance) with large numbers of beneficiaries and growing loan volumes. However, system-level reforms (legal frameworks, financial infrastructure, and market development) are progressing more slowly and remain the main constraint to achieving scale and sustainability.
1) Agricultural finance & smallholder access
The program made its strongest progress in expanding finance to smallholder farmers and agricultural value chains. Through commodity collateral financing CCF2 and digital platforms, farmers accessed loans using crops or produce as collateral, with an aggregated total from previous periods with ETB 2.5 billion (~US$23,2m- ETB 2.5 billion divided by the average exchange rate during each reporting period starting from 2021)
At the same time, digital models scaled rapidly: platforms like Lersha disbursed over 5,000 loans and registered more than 70,000 new farmers and mobilised loans to a value of US$ 441,000.
2) Movable asset-based lending (MABL)
This sector focuses on allowing borrowers, in particular small scale farmers, to use non-traditional collateral such as livestock or land-use rights. During the second half of 2025, the initiative moved from pilot to practical implementation: 127 farmers accessed loans (~US$131k) using livestock as collateral, supported by insurance, tagging, and a registry system.
While still small in scale, the results show proof of concept for expanding lending beyond traditional fixed assets. However, adoption by banks remains limited, and systems such as the collateral registry are not yet widely used.
3) Financial infrastructure & credit systems
Efforts in this area aim to strengthen the underlying systems that enable lending, such as credit bureaus and data infrastructure. Progress has been mixed.
On the positive side, the introduction of standardized reporting for digital loans generated significant new data, capturing over 639,000 borrowers and more than the advancement of digital lending. (Note: these results are not entirely directly associated with IFCs Access to Finance intervention)
However, key institutional reforms such as establishing a private credit bureau and upgrading the regulatory framework have been delayed due to procurement challenges and leadership changes. As a result, improvements in data availability are advancing faster than formal system reforms.
4) MSME finance and banking support The initiative supported banks to expand lending to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), including women-led businesses. Advisory support to Dashen Bank helped strengthen its MSME strategy, product offerings, and risk management. This contributed to growth in its MSME portfolio to over USD 170 million from a baseline of USD 129 million and expansion in the number of loans and products available to SMEs, (~USD 43 million)
While this shows progress in building institutional capacity, implementation has been slower than expected due to internal delays and the need for intensive technical support.
5) Capital markets development
Work in this sector is at an early stage and focuses on building the foundations for longer-term financing beyond bank lending. During the reporting period, activities concentrated on supporting government bond market reforms, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and developing an investor base. Concrete results in terms of actual bond issuance or capital raised remain limited, but key building blocks such as auction systems and market dialogue platforms have been established. Progress is therefore largely preparatory, with impacts expected over a longer time frame.
6) ESG integration (financial and real sectors)
This component aims to improve environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices in financial institutions and businesses, thereby supporting more sustainable investment. The program successfully delivered national ESG guidelines and extensive training, and influenced financing decisions (including around USD 120 million linked to improved ESG practices).
However, adoption by banks and firms remains gradual. The results suggest that while awareness and frameworks are in place, continued support is needed to translate them into consistent changes in lending and business practices.
Assessment
The A2F pillar achieved significant results, including around US$2.9 billion in financing , wide outreach to over 85,000 farmers and numerous MSMEs, and strong growth in digital and agri-finance models that demonstrated new lending approaches such as collateral- and value chain based finance.
However, progress on structural reforms and system adoption has been slower, and operational challenges particularly around KYC requirements and bank processes continue to constrain scaling.
